body:
Automations with Claude for a small business: 8 concrete examples. In a small business, a good automation with Claude is not a project of several months, but a workflow set up in an afternoon and then used every week.

None of the examples below runs without a human check step. All of them work with products that are already available, with no extra development.

Automations with Claude for a small business: 8 concrete examples

The eight examples below are grouped into four areas: customer communication, content and marketing, internal reports and, for businesses that have a developer, technical integrations. Each example shows what goes in, what comes out, what you see when the workflow really works and where mistakes most often appear.

You will not find figures here about time saved or money earned, because these differ from one business to another and cannot be supported without your own verified data.

What an automation with Claude actually means

Automations with Claude do not mean the assistant works alone, unsupervised. They mean a repetitive task gets a saved, tested prompt that you reuse every time instead of explaining the context from scratch again, as you would with a new colleague who does not yet know the company.

For anyone who has not yet used Claude in their business, the guide to what Claude AI is and how to use it explains the basic steps before moving on to repetitive workflows. A step that helps a lot at small businesses is gathering your own documents (policies, rates, sample replies) in a dedicated project, as described in organizing company documents in Claude projects, so that answers stay consistent no matter who asks the question and on what day of the week.

A working automation usually has three ingredients:

  • a saved prompt, tested on real cases, not improvised every time;
  • a correct data source: your own documents, an export from another tool or a spreadsheet;
  • a human step that approves the result before it reaches the customer or the public.

The absence of any one of the three ingredients quickly turns a time saving into a new source of work. An untested prompt produces inconsistent answers, a wrong data source produces wrong conclusions that are nicely worded, and the lack of human checking sometimes passes along a mistake that an attentive colleague would have caught in a few seconds.

The difference between a business that gains real time from Claude and one that merely experiments without results usually comes down to this minimal discipline: the prompt is written once, tested on a few difficult cases, not just on the simplest possible example, and only then goes into everyday use.

Automations for customer communication

Customer communication eats up time mainly through repetition: the same types of questions, the same situations of dissatisfaction, reworded from scratch every time.

Email triage and draft replies

Incoming emails are copied into a Claude project that already has access to the company policies (delivery terms, warranties, working hours). Claude proposes a category (technical question, complaint, quote request) and a draft reply in the company tone, with a direct reference to the relevant policy, not to a generic wording.

When the workflow works, the employee gets a draft they read in a few seconds, adjust where needed with details specific to the order and send, instead of starting from a blank page every time. The most common mistake appears when the project no longer has up-to-date policies: Claude keeps answering correctly in terms of grammar, but with old information about deadlines or rates, and the employee in a hurry no longer checks that detail.

Prepared replies to reviews, not improvised on the spot

Negative reviews often get a reply written in a hurry, under emotion, and the defensive tone is easily spotted by readers who look at reviews before choosing a business. A saved prompt, with verified examples like those in the template for replying to negative reviews, offers a calm starting point, structured around acknowledging the problem and the concrete next step.

The business owner reads the proposal, adds the detail specific to the situation (order number, product name) and publishes the final version. The most common risk is publishing the draft untouched, without the concrete detail that shows the customer they were really read, not just processed automatically.

Automations for content and marketing

Recurring content, the kind written every week or month, is where a well-built prompt pays for itself quickly, because the structure of the text stays the same and only the topic changes.

The social media content calendar

Starting from a list of topics and from the examples of prompts for Claude suited to each network, the business gets a first version for a whole month of posts, with length and tone adapted to each channel (more technical on LinkedIn, shorter on Facebook). The person in charge of social media selects, adjusts and schedules, rather than starting from a blank page every Monday morning.

When the automation goes well, next month's calendar already exists before the end of the current month. The problem appears when all the posts come out with the same sentence structure, a sign that the prompt was not varied enough, and the page's regular readers notice the repetitive pattern.

The first draft of blog articles

For businesses that keep a blog, the procedure described in how to write an article with Claude without it sounding generated can be turned into a repeated workflow: a short brief with the topic, keyword and target links, a first draft generated from your own materials, then human proofreading for substance and style before publishing. The editor remains the one who decides whether the text really answers the reader's question, not just whether it is grammatically correct.

Automations for reports and internal data

Periodic reports are a good candidate for automation, because the structure of the report repeats from one month to the next and only the figures behind it change.

The monthly summary from Search Console and Analytics

The CSV export from Search Console, combined with the observations from the site's free SEO tools, becomes the material that Claude turns into a summary by section: what went up, what went down, what is worth checking before the next meeting with the client or the manager. The person responsible for SEO validates the conclusions against the raw data before sending them on, because an incomplete export (for example, only the last 28 days instead of the requested period) can produce a summary that is well worded but based on wrong data.

Extracting data from invoices and documents

Supplier invoices or scanned documents, attached directly in the conversation, can be turned into tables with the relevant amounts and dates, ready to copy into your own records or into a spreadsheet. The workflow works well on clear, printed documents, and less reliably on blurry scans or unusual invoice formats. A check of the amounts is still mandatory before using them in accounting, because a reading error from a scanned document easily goes unnoticed if nobody compares the total with the original document.

Businesses that receive dozens of invoices a month gain the most from this workflow, because the time spent copying data manually grows in proportion to the number of documents, while checking the amounts already extracted stays quick. For low volume, a few invoices a week, the difference compared with direct manual entry is smaller.

Technical automations, for businesses with a developer

Businesses that already have a technical person can go a step further, with integrations that link Claude directly to internal tools, not just manual copying of text.

Connecting to internal tools through MCP

As described in the guide to MCP (Model Context Protocol), this protocol lets you connect Claude to your own databases, billing systems or a CRM, without building a separate integration from scratch for each tool. The initial setup requires a technical person, but daily use stays simple for the rest of the team, who just ask questions or request reports in plain language.

Small scripts with Claude Code, for repetitive tasks

For tasks such as bulk-renaming files, cleaning up an export or checking a set of addresses, a developer can ask Claude Code directly for a short script, tested first on a few rows before running it on the whole file. The basic rule stays the same as for any script written by someone else: test it on a copy, not on the original data.

How to organize your automations so they do not get out of hand

An automation that works well this month can produce mistakes next month if the company policy changes and the prompt stays out of date, and nobody knows any more who should review it.

  • keep prompts in one place, not scattered across messages and personal notes;
  • note the date each prompt was last checked and who is responsible for it;
  • never send a customer a result that a person has not read;
  • limit access to sensitive documents (contracts, payment data) strictly to what is needed for the task in question.

A prompt left unreviewed for several months usually ends up as a source of silent errors rather than a time-saving tool, especially if in the meantime the company has changed a supplier, a price or a warranty policy that the prompt still quotes from memory.

Conclusion

The eight examples above do not require a development budget, but the discipline of saving a good prompt instead of reinventing it every time. Businesses without a technical person can start with communication and content, and those with a developer can add integrations through MCP. If you need help setting up such a workflow around your website, our team answers on the contact page.
